name: Oysters / shellfish for zinc
lead: Oysters and other shellfish are eaten in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a concentrated food source of zinc, a mineral involved in testosterone production, skin health and hair. Followers eat them to support skin clarity, hair thickness and muscle-building hormones. Wikipedia describes oysters as having the highest zinc content of any common food, with two oysters (about 28 g) supplying the US reference daily intake.[1][2]

Zinc is required to make testosterone, and deficiency can lower it, delay puberty and cause hypogonadism.[2] Deficiency may also appear as acne, eczema, dry scaling skin, seborrheic dermatitis or thin, sparse hair, and may impair wound healing, which is why the mineral features in skin and hair discussions.[2] Meat, beans and nuts are also zinc sources, while phytates in whole grains bind zinc and reduce its absorption.[2]

A randomised trial reported that zinc-rich oysters, along with zinc-yeast and astaxanthin-enriched food, improved sleep efficiency and sleep onset in healthy adults.[3] The wider shellfish literature also covers food-safety topics such as Vibrio bacteria in raw oysters.[1][4]

angle.text: People eat oysters to make sure zinc intake is high, since zinc deficiency is linked with acne, thin hair and low testosterone. The looks payoff claimed is clearer skin, healthier hair and support for training results.

infobox: Iron, calcium, selenium, vitamin A, B12

paras: Oysters are described as an excellent source of zinc, iron, calcium, selenium, vitamin A and B12.[1] Beef, crab, lobster and pork are also zinc sources, while phytates in grains and legumes reduce zinc absorption.[1][2] A 1990 controlled trial in 18 healthy men fed several shellfish species and reported that oyster, clam, crab and mussel diets lowered VLDL triglycerides and cholesterol.[5]

Zinc is a catalytic and structural component of many enzymes, and deficiency can reduce testosterone and delay puberty.[2] Skin and hair signs of deficiency include acne, eczema, xerosis, seborrheic dermatitis and sparse hair, and wound healing may be impaired.[2] Followers therefore treat zinc-rich foods as a way to keep those systems well supplied.
Zinc deficiency affects an estimated 2.2 billion people worldwide.[2] Reference sources tie the benefits of zinc to correcting low intake rather than to intake above sufficiency.

As filter feeders, oysters can concentrate Vibrio vulnificus and V. parahaemolyticus, mainly dangerous to immunocompromised people, and shucking cuts can lead to cellulitis.[1] Reviews describe vibriosis as an infection group ranging from mild illness to necrotizing fasciitis, mostly following contact with marine environments or shellfish, especially oysters.[4] A 2016 review discusses managing Vibrio risk in raw oysters.[6]
Shellfish allergy is among the more common food allergies and ranges from hives to anaphylaxis.[7]
No studies found on oyster or shellfish consumption and appearance outcomes. Related trials include zinc-rich oysters and sleep in healthy adults[3] and shellfish and blood lipids in men.[5]

card.summary: Oysters are the richest food source of zinc, used as a T-support food; benefit is tied to correcting deficiency.
card.note: Raw shellfish carries Vibrio and other food-safety risks.

quick.overview:
Oysters pack more zinc than any common food, so they are favoured by people trying to support testosterone.

Zinc deficiency can lower testosterone, but the sources say supplementing beyond sufficiency has no effect on serum testosterone.
quick.mechanism: Zinc is needed for testosterone synthesis and many enzymes; oysters simply supply it in food form.
quick.risks: Raw oysters can carry dangerous bacteria, especially for immunocompromised people.
